title: The Mystery of the Missing Sandwich

pages.text: The Mystery of the Missing Sandwich A Story About Bacteria It was Science Fair Week at Riverside School. Lila and her best friend Jay were decorating their classroom. Jay reached into his backpack. "My sandwich!" He had forgotten it there all weekend. The bread smelled strange. Tiny fuzzy patches had appeared. Lila stepped back. "Eww! What happened to it?" Just then, their science teacher, Ms. Rivera, walked over with a smile. "I think you've just discovered a tiny world that you can't even see." Did You Know? Bacteria are tiny living things. You need a microscope to see them!

The Invisible World A Story About Bacteria Ms. Rivera placed a sandwich crumb under the microscope. Lila and Jay took turns looking through the eyepiece. They were amazed by thousands of tiny little dots. Ms. Rivera explained that these are bacteria—tiny living organisms found everywhere, from soil to skin. Lila called it an invisible city. Did You Know? Bacteria are so tiny that millions of them can fit on the tip of your finger!

The Fastest Growing Town A Story About Bacteria Ms. Rivera explained binary fission: one bacterium copies itself and splits, and this process repeats, allowing one tiny bacterium to become millions. That is why food left out too long becomes covered in bacteria. Did You Know? Bacteria reproduce very fast! In the right conditions, one bacterium can become more than 1 million bacteria in just 24 hours.

Good and Bad Neighbors A Story About Bacteria "Not all bacteria are the same," Ms. Rivera explained. "Many bacteria help us, like the ones used to make yogurt. But some bacteria can spoil food or make people sick." Bacteria can cause illnesses such as strep throat, staph infections, and some kinds of food poisoning caused by bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella. Some bacteria can also cause dental cavities if we don't brush our teeth. So we wash our hands, keep food in the refrigerator, brush our teeth, and throw away spoiled food. Jay nodded. "So bacteria aren't the enemy. We just need to stop the harmful ones." Did You Know? Good habits help keep harmful bacteria away!

Tiny Scientists A Story About Bacteria For the Science Fair, Lila and Jay built a giant model of a bacterium. They also made a simple display showing binary fission. One bacterium became two. Two became four. Four became eight. Soon the chart was filled with tiny circles. Their classmates gathered around. "I never knew bacteria were living things," one student said. "They're tiny... but they can have a big impact." Lila smiled. "Sometimes the smallest discoveries are the biggest surprises."

Science Element: Bacteria Bacteria are tiny single-celled living organisms. Millions of them can fit on the tip of your finger. Most bacteria are harmless, and many are helpful. Some bacteria can spoil food or make people sick. Bacteria reproduce by a process called binary fission. Examples of bacterial diseases include strep throat, staph infections, food poisoning, and dental cavities. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections by killing bacteria or stopping their growth, but antibiotics do not work against viruses. Stay healthy by washing hands, refrigerating food, washing fruits and vegetables, brushing and flossing, and throwing away spoiled food. Remember: Bacteria are part of the invisible world all around us. Most are harmless, many are helpful, and learning how to stop harmful bacteria helps keep us healthy.
